div.p: Background. Extensive surgical resection is associated with longer survival in patients with glioma; however, the combined impact of surgical extent and molecular pathology on prognosis remains unclear. In this study, we evaluated how molecular pathology and clinical features influence surgical outcomes in patients with World Health Organization (WHO) grade 4 gliomas, including isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant astrocytomas and IDH wildtype glioblastomas. Methods. Data from 501 patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas who underwent surgery were obtained from the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas database (2005-2019). The effect of resection extent on overall survival was analyzed and stratified using molecular pathology and clinical characteristics. Survival differences were assessed using the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test, and prognostic factors were identified through univariate and multivariate analyses. Results. The extent of resection significantly influenced survival, but its impact varied by molecular subtype. In WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas, gross total resection (GTR) did not confer a significant survival advantage over subtotal resection (STR). Among glioblastoma patients, those with non-methylated O-(6)-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase promoters and preoperative Karnofsky Performance Status ≤80 showed no significant benefit from GTR compared to STR, whereas GTR substantially prolonged survival in other subgroups. Conclusions. The survival benefits of extensive resection vary among patients with WHO grade 4 glioma. Molecular pathology and clinical characteristics should be considered in surgical planning. A conservative approach may be appropriate for some patients; nevertheless, a more aggressive strategy may optimize survival and quality of life for others.

Glioblastoma, the most common malignant tumor of the central nervous system, has a median survival of only 14-17 months. [1][2][3] Molecular markers, including isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutations and 1p/19q codeletion, are critical prognostic factors that influence the biological behavior of gliomas. [4][5][6] In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) reclassified central nervous system tumors, designating IDH-mutant glioblastoma as astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4, and reserving the term "glioblastoma" for IDH wildtype WHO grade 4 gliomas. 7 In this reclassification, the importance of molecular pathology in glioma diagnosis and prognosis was emphasized.

The standard treatment for glioblastoma includes surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and temozolomide chemotherapy. 8 Maximal safe resection of the T1-weighted contrast-enhanced tumor is preferred, as it is strongly associated with improved survival outcomes. [9][10][11][12] However, postoperative neurological deficits can negatively impact prognosis, 13 presenting a significant challenge in balancing the extent of resection with the preservation of neurological function. Moreover, if extending resection does not substantially improve overall survival but increases the risk of neurological deficits in specific molecular subtypes of glioblastoma, a more conservative surgical strategy with a focus on preserving neurological function may be appropriate.

The prognostic significance of surgical resection extent across glioblastoma subtypes remains unclear. Patients with IDH wild-type gliomas generally have a poorer prognosis than those with IDH-mutant gliomas. 4,14,15 Some studies suggest that more extensive resection may benefit patients with IDH-mutant high-grade gliomas (WHO grade III-IV), whereas extending resection beyond non-enhancing regions may not offer additional survival benefits for IDH wild-type gliomas. 16 Conversely, other studies have found that extensive resection significantly prolongs overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) in IDH wild-type glioblastoma, supporting a more aggressive surgical approach for this subtype. 17 These findings indicate that the prognostic impact of resection extent may vary depending on the molecular profile of WHO grade 4 gliomas.

We conducted this study to determine whether the extent of contrast-enhanced tumor resection influences prognosis in WHO grade 4 gliomas, including IDH-mutant astrocytomas and IDH-wildtype glioblastomas. The analysis focused on the resection of gadolinium-enhancing tumor tissue, whereas supramarginal resection of non-enhancing FLAIR-hyperintense regions was not systematically evaluated. Additionally, we considered the influence of additional factors, such as O(6)-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation status and clinical characteristics, including preoperative Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), to assess the prognostic value of resection extent across different subgroups.

Molecular pathology-guided surgical resection is not yet feasible in clinical practice; however, artificial intelligence-driven analysis of radiomic features may provide molecular insights. [18][19][20][21][22] Furthermore, rapid intraoperative pathological techniques, such as Raman spectroscopy, offer the possibility of real-time molecular diagnosis. [23][24][25] In the future, molecular pathology-guided resection could become a reality in surgical interventions.

We hypothesize that not all WHO grade 4 gliomas will benefit equally from extensive resection. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed the prognostic role of resection extent within various subgroups using data collected from the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA) database.

div.head: Patients
div.p: In this study, we retrospectively analyzed 963 patients who underwent surgical treatment for WHO grade 4 gliomas at Beijing Tiantan Hospital, affiliated with Capital Medical University, between March 2005 and February 2019. Clinical characteristics, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, histopathology, molecular pathology information, postoperative adjuvant therapy, and follow-up data were collected from the CGGA database (http://www.cgga.org.cn). 26 Informed consent was obtained from all patients. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Tiantan Hospital.

Inclusion criteria were as follows: patients aged ≥18 years; those undergoing their first surgical treatment; pathologically diagnosed with WHO grade 4 glioma according to the 2021 WHO Central Nervous System Tumor Classification; availability of molecular pathology data (including IDH, 1p/19q, and MGMT promoter mutation status); preoperative and

div.head: Importance of the Study
div.p: This study clarifies how the extent of resection affects survival in WHO grade 4 gliomas across different molecular subtypes, addressing a gap in prior research that often overlooked molecular distinctions. We demonstrate that gross total resection offers no survival advantage over subtotal resection in WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas or in glioblastomas with non-methylated O-(6)-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase promoters and preoperative Karnofsky Performance Status ≤ 80, whereas GTR substantially prolonged survival in other subgroups. This finding challenges the one-size-fits-all approach to glioma surgery and highlights the need for personalized treatment strategies. Our work provides critical evidence for neurosurgeons to optimize surgical planning, balancing tumor resection and neurological preservation. Future research can build on this to develop molecular pathology-guided surgical protocols and further refine prognostic models for glioma patients, potentially improving both survival rates and quality of life.

The extent of tumor resection (EOR) was determined by comparing preoperative MR images with postoperative ones obtained within 72 hours after the surgery. 27 Tumor volume was measured using the freely accessible software MRIcro (http://www.mccauslandcenter.sc.edu/mricro/). The EOR, defined as the reduction in contrast-enhanced tumor volume, was evaluated by comparing preoperative and postoperative contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI images, calculated as:

div.p: ) . 28 Gross total resection (GTR) was radiologically defined as the complete absence of contrast-enhanced lesions on postoperative MRI, indicating 100% removal of all visible contrast-enhancing tumor components. Subtotal resection (STR) was characterized by a 90% to <100% volumetric reduction of the contrast-enhancing tumor mass, while partial resection (PR) referred to surgical removal encompassing less than 90% of the enhancing tumor volume. [29][30][31] Cases in which the resection margin extended >2 cm beyond the contrast-enhancing tumor border were excluded, as these were classified as supramarginal resections and thus lay outside the scope of the present analysis. 32

div.head: Molecular Analysis
div.p: Molecular pathology data were obtained from the CGGA database. Post-surgery tumor tissues were subjected to molecular pathology testing, with IDH mutation and MGMT promoter methylation status determined via DNA pyrosequencing. 33,34 Following the 2021 WHO Classification of Central Nervous System Tumors, the WHO grade 4 glioma cases were classified into two subgroups: (1) Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4, and (2) Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4.

div.head: Statistical Analysis
div.p: Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were presented as medians and interquartile ranges. Differences in clinical characteristics between cohorts were compared using unpaired t-tests and chi-square tests, with Fisher's exact test applied when chi-square test assumptions were not met. OS was defined as the time from the first surgery to death or last follow-up, and PFS was defined as the time from primary surgery to the first clinical or radiological progression, death, or last follow-up. OS and PFS were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method and survival curves were compared using the log-rank test. Furthermore, univariate analysis was conducted to evaluate the prognostic significance of variables, while multivariate survival analysis of relevant factors (including sex, age, preoperative KPS, molecular subtypes, MGMT methylation status, EOR, and postoperative adjuvant therapy) was performed using the Cox proportional hazards model. A P-value < .05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (v 4.1.0, The R Foundation, Vienna, Austria) and GraphPad Prism 8.3 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA).

div.head: Patient Characteristics
div.p: Overall, 963 cases of WHO grade 4 glioma were retrieved from the CGGA database (Figure 1). After excluding 462 patients (11 patients aged < 18 years, 355 with recurrent glioma, 27 lacking follow-up information, and 69 with incomplete molecular pathology data), 501 patients were included in the analysis. Table 1 summarizes the clinical characteristics of all patients. Among the 501 patients, 302 were male (62.3%), and 199 were female (37.7%), with a median age of 52 years (interquartile range [IQR], 42-59 years). The median preoperative KPS was 90 (IQR: 80-90). Among these patients, 90 (18%) had astrocytoma and 411 (82%) had glioblastoma. The primary clinical symptoms were headache (65.9%) and neurological dysfunction (42.1%). Furthermore, patients with astrocytoma were younger than those with glioblastoma (P < .0001), and their initial symptoms differed (P = .043), with a higher incidence of epilepsy in patients with astrocytoma (25.6% vs. 9.2%). Patients with astrocytoma had a higher preoperative KPS than those with glioblastoma (P = .041). Tumor location differed significantly between astrocytoma and glioblastoma (P < .0001). WHO grade 4 astrocytomas were predominantly situated in the frontal lobe, while glioblastomas more often invaded the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, as well as deep brain structures. Consequently, WHO grade 4 astrocytomas were more amenable to GTR. Additionally, the proportion of patients with MGMT promoter methylation was significantly higher in the WHO grade 4 astrocytoma group than in the glioblastoma group (65.5% vs. 45.6%, P = .001). Compared with patients who underwent GTR, those who underwent subtotal or partial resection had more aggressive invasion of deep brain structures (P < .0001) (Table 2).

div.head: Survival Analysis
div.p: The median follow-up time of all patients was 45.4 months. Patients who were still alive at last follow-up (n = 121) had a median follow-up time of 24 months. The median OS of all patients was 16 months. No surgery-related deaths occurred. The OS of patients with glioblastoma was significantly shorter than that of patients with WHO grade 4 astrocytoma (hazard ratio [HR]: 2.20, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.73-2.78, 14.1 months vs 34.2 months, P < .0001).

We analyzed the impact of EOR on OS in patients with grade 4 glioma (Figure 2). Patients who underwent GTR demonstrated significantly longer OS and PFS than those who underwent STR or PR (both P < .0001). After molecular pathological classification, increasing EOR resulted in longer OS and PFS in patients with glioblastoma (both P < .0001).

However, in patients with WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, OS (42.3 months vs 35.8 months, P = .4172) and PFS (34.2 months vs 23.6 months, P = .5767) did not differ significantly between those who underwent GTR or STR.

In the univariate survival analysis of all the patients, the following were identified as statistically significant prognostic factors for OS: age (HR: 1.107, P < .0001), preoperative KPS (≤ 80 vs > 80; HR: 1.349; P = .004), EOR (non-GTR vs GTR; HR: 2.945; P < .0001), molecular subtype (glioblastoma vs. astrocytoma; HR: 2.224; P < .0001), MGMT promoter methylation status (non-methylated vs methylated; HR: 1.264; P = .026), and the adjuvant therapy (no vs yes; HR: 4.61; P < .0001) (Table S1 in Online Resource 1). Similarly, Cox multivariate analysis showed that adjuvant therapy (no vs yes; HR: 4.254; P < .0001), molecular subtype (glioblastoma vs astrocytoma; HR: 2.135; P < .0001), MGMT promoter methylation status (non-methylated vs methylated; HR: 1.299; P = .026), preoperative KPS (≤ 80 vs > 80; HR: 1.307; P = .017), and EOR (non-GTR vs GTR; HR: 2.842; P < .0001) were independent prognostic factors for OS in all patients with grade 4 glioma (Table S2 in Online Resource 1).

Multivariate analysis in the WHO grade 4 astrocytoma group revealed that adjuvant therapy (no vs. yes; HR: 8.356; P < .0001), MGMT promoter methylation status (non-methylated vs. methylated; HR: 1.983; P = .039), and EOR (non-GTR vs GTR; HR: 2.768; P = .002) were significant prognostic factors for OS. Conversely, in the glioblastoma group, age (HR: 1.018, P = .001), adjuvant therapy (no vs yes; HR: 3.526; P < .0001), and EOR (non-GTR vs GTR; HR: 3.134; P < .0001) were independent prognostic factors for OS (Table 3).

div.head: Impact of EOR in Subgroups of WHO Grade 4 Gliomas
div.p: We further stratified WHO grade 4 gliomas based on clinical and molecular pathological features to evaluate the impact of EOR on OS across different subgroups (Figure 3). In WHO grade 4 astrocytomas, OS did not differ significantly between GTR and STR, regardless of MGMT promoter methylation status (non-methylated: P = .6375; methylated: P = .4915) or preoperative KPS (≤ 80: P = .6072; > 80: P = .2656).

For glioblastomas with non-methylated MGMT promoters and preoperative KPS ≤ 80, there was no significant difference in OS between GTR and STR (P = .2168). However, in patients with glioblastoma with non-methylated MGMT promoters and preoperative KPS > 80, as well as those with methylated MGMT promoters, GTR significantly prolonged OS compared with STR (all P-values < .0001), highlighting the survival benefit of extensive resection in these subgroups.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Glioblastoma, the most common primary brain tumor, is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Surgical resection remains a cornerstone of glioma treatment and extensive studies have shown that greater resection extent is associated with longer survival. div.head: Neuro-Oncology Advances
div.p: Hou et al.: Surgical resection impact on WHO grade 4 gliomas survival preservation is crucial. The importance of IDH mutation status in glioma diagnosis and prognosis has become evident with the advent of molecular pathology; therefore, it is essential to reassess the impact of resection extent on survival across different molecular subtypes of WHO grade 4 gliomas.

In this study, WHO grade 4 astrocytoma showed substantially longer OS than IDH wild-type glioblastoma, in line with previous reports. 1,4,36,37 We further demonstrated that resection extent is significantly correlated with survival; however, this relationship varies by molecular subtype. In IDH wildtype glioblastoma, greater resection extent significantly improves OS and PFS. Among WHO grade 4 astrocytomas, GTR confers a significant OS advantage over non-GTR (encompassing both subtotal and partial resection). In contrast, when GTR is compared directly to STR alone, the difference in OS is not statistically significant, implying that STR may offer survival outcomes comparable to those achieved with GTR in this setting. This finding aligns with those highlighted by Beiko et al, 16 who showed that in IDH wild-type gliomas, patients with no residual enhanced tumor had longer median survival than those with residual tumors. Similarly, Gessler et al 38 found that complete resection and MGMT promoter methylation were associated with better prognosis. Marchi et al 39 further supported positive impact of complete resection on survival, noting that the prognostic value of MGMT methylation was less pronounced in completely resected cases. Surgical resection, patient age, preoperative KPS, postoperative adjuvant therapy, and MGMT promoter methylation are all significant prognostic factors for glioblastoma. 1,35,[40][41][42] However, when considering both molecular and clinical features, the precise impact of resection extent on prognosis remains unclear. Molinaro et al 36 were the first to integrate resection extent, clinical factors, and molecular features to assess glioblastoma prognosis. Their findings revealed that for patients aged ≤ 65 years, resection of both contrast-enhanced and non-contrast-enhanced tumors was associated with longer survival, regardless of IDH and MGMT status. In contrast, for patients aged > 65 years with IDH wild-type glioblastoma, complete resection of enhanced tumors improved survival, but further resection of non-enhanced tumors provided no additional benefit.

We further explored the interaction between clinical characteristics, surgical resection, and molecular pathological features. By stratifying patients based on IDH mutation status, subsequently MGMT methylation status, and finally preoperative KPS, we found that in WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas, there was no significant difference in survival between complete and subtotal resection. Additionally, in IDH wild-type glioblastoma, patients with MGMT methylation had significantly prolonged survival with more extensive resection. Among patients with MGMT non-methylation, those with preoperative KPS ≤ 80 showed no significant difference in survival between GTR and STR, while those with KPS > 80 had significantly prolonged survival with GTR.

Based on these findings, we recommend a conservative surgical strategy for patients with WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma and IDH wild-type glioblastoma with preoperative KPS ≤ 80 and MGMT methylation. For these patients, the extent of resection should aim for STR rather than striving for GTR, especially for tumors located in eloquent areas, as complete resection does not significantly improve survival in these groups while potentially increasing the risk of neurological deficits. For other IDH wild-type glioblastomas, we advocate for an aggressive surgical strategy to achieve complete tumor resection, including expanding resection in non-functional areas. 31 Surgical planning for WHO grade 4 gliomas should fully consider both clinical and molecular pathological features to maximize patient survival benefits.

Currently, molecular pathological information is typically obtained postoperatively, limiting its use in guiding surgical decisions. However, advancements in preoperative molecular imaging and intraoperative rapid molecular pathological detection, such as artificial intelligence-driven radiomic analysis and Raman spectroscopy, offer the potential for real-time molecular diagnosis. These technologies could enable molecular pathology-guided surgical resection, which we propose as a novel concept to improve patient survival outcomes. Future research should focus on developing and validating these individualized surgical strategies based on molecular pathological features.

Nevertheless, our study had several limitations that warrant consideration. As a retrospective study, our research may have inherent selection bias. Not all newly diagnosed patients with WHO grade 4 glioma underwent surgical treatment, and resection extent decisions were made without a pathological diagnosis. Additionally, the number of patients in each group was imbalanced, and postoperative treatments and follow-up varied. Since we only included cases from a single center, sample bias cannot be excluded. Therefore, larger datasets and multicenter studies with

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This study underscores the importance of incorporating both molecular pathological features and clinical characteristics when assessing the prognostic value of surgical resection in WHO grade 4 gliomas. Extensive resection offers survival benefits for patients with IDH wild-type glioblastoma, particularly those with MGMT promoter methylation and higher preoperative KPS scores; however, it does not provide significant survival advantages for patients with WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas or those with lower KPS scores and non-methylated MGMT promoters. These findings highlight the need for individualized surgical strategies that balance resection extent with the preservation of neurological function, aiming to optimize both survival and quality of life. Future prospective studies and multicenter collaborations are essential to validate these findings and refine surgical guidelines for glioma treatment.

div.head: Lay Summary
div.p: Gliomas are brain tumors, and people with more of the tumor removed during surgery often live longer. The authors of this study wanted to find out how the type of tumor and a person's overall health affect the benefits of removing more of the tumor. To do this, they looked at records from 501 people with the most aggressive types of glioma who had brain surgery, and they compared how much tumor was removed with how long each person lived. Their results showed that removing the entire tumor helped people live longer in many cases, but the benefit depended on the type of tumor and the person's condition before surgery.
